body:
From social reform to political participation

During the nineteenth century, reformers challenged practices that restricted women's education and freedom. Women themselves increasingly founded schools, published writings and organised associations.

This activity provided experience in public speaking, administration and collective action. By the early twentieth century, women's movements were demanding not only education and social reform but also political rights, including the right to vote.

Important women's organisations

Women's Indian Association, 1917

The Women's Indian Association (WIA) was founded in 1917 through the efforts of Annie Besant, Margaret Cousins and Dorothy Jinarajadasa. It campaigned for women's political rights and social improvement.

All India Women's Conference, 1927

The All India Women's Conference (AIWC) was established in 1927, with its first conference held at Poona. Margaret Cousins was important in its establishment.

The organisation initially emphasised women's education and later took up wider demands involving marriage reform, legal rights and social equality. It was not simply a branch of the Indian National Congress.

Women in Congress leadership

Annie Besant became the first woman president of the Indian National Congress at the Calcutta session in 1917. She was British-born and had been active in the Home Rule movement.

Sarojini Naidu became the first Indian woman president of the Indian National Congress at the Kanpur session in 1925.

Annie Besant, 1917: first woman Congress president. Sarojini Naidu, 1925: first Indian woman Congress president. The word Indian changes the answer.

Women in the Civil Disobedience Movement

The Salt Satyagraha of 1930 created opportunities for women to participate directly in mass protest. Women marched, made salt in defiance of colonial regulations, picketed foreign cloth and liquor shops, and accepted imprisonment.

Women's participation was particularly visible during the Civil Disobedience Movement. Some urban participants came from educated or relatively privileged families, while many rural women joined through their households and local communities.

Participation was not confined to one class or community. However, opportunities for public leadership were unequal, and women's increased presence in demonstrations did not automatically produce equal authority inside political organisations.

Women in the Quit India Movement, 1942

When the Quit India Movement began in August 1942, the arrest of senior nationalist leaders created opportunities for other organisers to take responsibility.

Aruna Asaf Ali became associated with the raising of the national flag at Gowalia Tank Maidan, Bombay, on 9 August 1942.

Usha Mehta, a young nationalist from Gujarat, helped operate the clandestine Congress Radio during the Quit India Movement. Underground broadcasting allowed messages about nationalist activity to circulate despite government restrictions.

These examples demonstrate that women participated not only in public marches but also in political communication, organisation and underground resistance.

Participation and social constraints

Nationalist leaders frequently praised women for sacrifice, courage and service. Yet conventional expectations concerning marriage, domestic responsibilities and acceptable public behaviour often remained powerful. Many women had limited access to education, independent income or positions of political authority.

Women's organisations therefore continued to work for rights beyond the immediate goal of ending colonial rule. The national movement and the struggle for women's equality overlapped but were not identical.

Prelims focus

  • Women's Indian Association: established in 1917.
  • All India Women's Conference: first conference at Poona in 1927.
  • Annie Besant: first woman Congress president, Calcutta, 1917.
  • Sarojini Naidu: first Indian woman Congress president, Kanpur, 1925.
  • Women participated in salt-making, picketing and demonstrations during Civil Disobedience.
  • Aruna Asaf Ali and Usha Mehta are associated with the Quit India Movement of 1942.
  • Trap: Increased participation in protests did not mean equal representation in political leadership.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, 2020–21 edition, chapter Women, Caste and Reform, printed pp. 94–101; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, chapter Nationalism in India, printed pp. 66–68; NCERT, Women's Movements in India: Tracing the Journey, section Voting Rights for Women and Women's Indian Association, consulted 22 November 2026; Indian National Congress, biography Annie Besant and historical account The Women Presidents of INC, consulted 22 November 2026; The Indian Express, The Story of Usha Mehta and Congress Radio, 22 March 2024, consulted 22 November 2026.]

title: Women's Participation, Organisations and Political Leadership

body:
Why education became a political issue

Colonial educational institutions were connected with government authority. Nationalist leaders argued that education should also develop public responsibility, Indian languages, self-reliance and commitment to national service.

Students could contribute to the national movement by organising meetings, distributing literature, participating in demonstrations and refusing cooperation with institutions under colonial control. Their participation was shaped by the availability of alternative schools and by family circumstances.

Swadeshi and national education after 1905

The Swadeshi Movement gained strength after the partition of Bengal in 1905. Boycott was directed not only at foreign goods but also at selected colonial institutions.

National education became a major objective. Supporters established or promoted Indian educational institutions intended to reduce dependence on colonial control. The National Council of Education was established in Bengal in 1906 as part of this wider effort.

Students during Non-Cooperation, 1920–1922

Gandhi's Non-Cooperation programme called for the boycott of government-controlled educational institutions. During 1921, thousands of students left such schools and colleges. Some teachers and headmasters also resigned.

However, leaving an institution did not automatically provide another place to study. Alternative colleges required buildings, teachers and financial support. Because national institutions were not available everywhere, some students later returned to government-controlled education.

This illustrates an important limitation: the success of an educational boycott depended partly on whether practical alternatives could be provided.

Gujarat Vidyapith, 1920

Gujarat Vidyapith was founded at Ahmedabad on 18 October 1920 under the guidance of Mahatma Gandhi. It emerged from the national education movement associated with Non-Cooperation.

The institution aimed to combine education with self-reliance, productive work, social service, use of Indian languages and national reconstruction. It provided an alternative to dependence on government-controlled education.

Gujarat Vidyapith is a major Gujarat example of the educational dimension of the freedom struggle. Its founding year is 1920, not 1930 or 1942.

All India Students Federation, 1936

The All India Students Federation (AISF) emerged in 1936 as an attempt to coordinate student organisations at the national level. It reflected the growing importance of students as an organised political group.

Student organisations were not politically uniform. Their leaders and members held different views, and wider political disagreements also affected student activity.

Students and the Quit India Movement, 1942

The Quit India Movement of 1942 involved students and young activists in demonstrations, distribution of information and underground political work. The detention of senior leaders increased the importance of local organisation and communication.

Some students interrupted their studies or risked disciplinary action and imprisonment. Their contribution therefore included both visible demonstrations and less visible organisational tasks.

Distinguishing student activity from youth leadership

A student movement is organised primarily around students or educational institutions. A youth-led political action may include people of student age who are no longer enrolled in formal education. Both contributed to the freedom struggle, but they are not interchangeable categories.

Similarly, leaving a government school during Non-Cooperation was a boycott of colonial institutions; joining an underground network in 1942 was a different form of political resistance.

Prelims focus

  • Swadeshi Movement: strengthened after the partition of Bengal in 1905.
  • National Council of Education: established in Bengal in 1906.
  • Gujarat Vidyapith: founded by Gandhi at Ahmedabad on 18 October 1920.
  • Students boycotted government-controlled educational institutions during Non-Cooperation.
  • All India Students Federation: emerged in 1936.
  • Students contributed to demonstrations and underground activity during Quit India in 1942.
  • Trap: The educational boycott and the establishment of alternative national institutions were related but different activities.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, 2020–21 edition, chapter The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947, printed pp. 113–118; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, chapter Nationalism in India, printed pp. 57–58; Gujarat Vidyapith, official institutional history and Journey, 1920–1930, entries for 18 October 1920, consulted 22 November 2026; Gandhi Heritage Portal, Gujarat Vidyapith, Ahmedabad, institutional history, consulted 22 November 2026; Tom Wilkinson, Student Politics in British India and Beyond: The Rise and Fragmentation of the All India Student Federation, 1936–1950, South Asia Multidisciplinary Academic Journal, 2019, abstract and introductory discussion, consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Four stages connect the 1905 boycott, national institutions in 1906 and 1920, student organisation in 1936, and Quit India resistance in 1942.
pictures.caption: Nationalist education developed from boycotts into independent institutions and student organisations.

title: Students, National Education and Youth in the Freedom Struggle

body:
National freedom and social equality

British rule was not the only source of injustice experienced by Indians. Caste discrimination restricted access to schools, wells, temples, public places and occupations. Some communities also lacked effective representation in political institutions.

For this reason, the demand for independence and the struggle against social inequality were closely connected but not identical. Several leaders argued that political freedom would be incomplete unless oppressed communities gained equality, dignity and a voice in government.

Non-Brahmin and anti-caste organisation

Jyotirao Phule established the Satyashodhak Samaj in 1873 in Maharashtra. It challenged caste hierarchy and promoted social equality and education.

In the Madras Presidency, non-Brahmin political organisation developed through the Justice Party, associated with the South Indian Liberal Federation formed in 1916. The party regarded participation in representative institutions as a means of securing political opportunities for non-Brahmin communities.

During the Non-Cooperation period, the Justice Party did not follow the Congress boycott of elections to the Madras legislative council. It considered participation useful for gaining access to power from which non-Brahmin groups had often been excluded.

E. V. Ramasamy, known as Periyar, launched the Self-Respect Movement in 1925 in the Tamil region. It opposed caste hierarchy and emphasised dignity, social equality and reform of practices that restricted women's freedom.

These movements show that marginalised groups did not always accept the Congress programme as the only path to political or social change.

B. R. Ambedkar and Dalit political organisation

Dr B. R. Ambedkar argued that oppressed communities needed education, social rights and effective political representation. His organisations and campaigns addressed discrimination directly.

  • Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha, 1924: Established to promote education and the welfare of socially excluded communities.
  • Mahad Satyagraha, 1927: Asserted the right of excluded communities to use a public water tank at Mahad in present-day Maharashtra.
  • Kalaram Temple entry movement, 1930: Challenged restrictions on temple entry at Nashik.
  • Depressed Classes Association, 1930: Associated with Ambedkar's efforts to organise the Depressed Classes and secure their political interests.

These campaigns were not simply requests for sympathy. They asserted that access to public resources and independent political organisation were essential for equal citizenship.

Gandhi, Ambedkar and the Poona Pact of 1932

Gandhi campaigned against untouchability and supported access to public wells, roads, schools and temples. Ambedkar placed particular emphasis on the ability of Dalits to select representatives who would defend their interests.

The disagreement became especially important over the question of separate electorates. Under a separate electorate, voters belonging to a specified community elect representatives through an electoral arrangement limited to that community.

The British Communal Award of 1932 provided for separate electorates for the Depressed Classes. Gandhi opposed this arrangement, while Ambedkar considered independent political representation necessary to safeguard Dalit interests.

The resulting Poona Pact of September 1932 provided reserved legislative seats within a joint electorate instead of separate electorates. Under the Pact's agreed procedure, voters belonging to the Depressed Classes first selected a panel of candidates for reserved seats; the final election was conducted by the wider general electorate.

The Pact provided 148 reserved seats in provincial legislatures, along with provisions for representation in the central legislature. This arrangement was a historical agreement for the institutions of that period; it should not be confused with the later constitutional system of representation in independent India.

Reserved seats specify seats to be filled by candidates from a particular community. A separate electorate restricts who votes to choose those representatives. The two arrangements are not synonymous. The Poona Pact replaced the proposed separate electorates for the Depressed Classes with reserved seats under joint electorates.

Muslim participation and the problem of representation

Religious communities were not politically uniform. Muslim participation in the freedom struggle included both cooperation with Congress-led campaigns and independent political organisations.

The Khilafat Committee was formed in Bombay in March 1919. Leaders such as Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali worked with Gandhi to connect the Khilafat agitation with the Non-Cooperation Movement during 1920–1922.

In the North-West Frontier Province, Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan developed the Khudai Khidmatgar movement, whose volunteers were also called Red Shirts. It became associated with non-violent resistance and participated in the Civil Disobedience agitation, including protests around Peshawar in 1930.

At the same time, some Muslim political organisations remained cautious about Congress leadership, particularly over questions of political representation and minority rights. This means that neither complete unity nor complete non-participation accurately describes Muslim political activity.

Understanding historical visibility

Prominent national leaders are important for understanding the movement, but they did not act alone. Women organised marches and communication; peasants sustained village campaigns; workers conducted strikes; students distributed information; and tribal communities defended land and forest rights.

Social barriers influenced who gained formal recognition. Women, agricultural labourers, Dalits, tribal participants and local organisers were not always equally represented in leadership positions. Their participation nevertheless helped determine the scale and character of the national movement.

One-glance comparison of major forms of participation

Group or movementMain concernImportant example
Peasant satyagrahaRevenue or planter exploitationKheda, 1918; Bardoli, 1928
Organised peasant movementTenancy and agrarian rightsAll India Kisan Sabha, 1936
Tribal resistanceLand, forest and forced labourBirsa Munda; Eki Movement
Industrial labourWages and working conditionsAITUC, 1920
Women's political actionNational freedom and social rightsWIA, 1917; Salt Satyagraha, 1930
Student movementNational education and protestGujarat Vidyapith, 1920
Dalit assertionEquality and political representationMahad, 1927; Poona Pact, 1932

Prelims focus

  • Satyashodhak Samaj: Jyotirao Phule, 1873.
  • Self-Respect Movement: E. V. Ramasamy, 1925.
  • Mahad Satyagraha: B. R. Ambedkar, 1927; public water access.
  • Poona Pact: September 1932; reserved seats within joint electorates for the Depressed Classes.
  • Khilafat agitation: Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali; cooperation with Non-Cooperation.
  • Khudai Khidmatgar: Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan; North-West Frontier Province.
  • Trap: Reserved seats within a joint electorate do not constitute a separate electorate.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, 2020–21 edition, chapter Women, Caste and Reform, printed pp. 100–108; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, chapter Nationalism in India, printed pp. 55–58 and 67–69; Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches, Government of Maharashtra, vol. 8, Appendix XX, Poona Pact, clauses 1–3, consulted 22 November 2026; Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar Samata Pratishthan, About Dr Ambedkar, section on Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha, consulted 22 November 2026; Tamil Nadu History Congress, The Self-Respect Movement of Periyar, section on its founding in 1925, consulted 22 November 2026; IGNOU, Civil Disobedience Movement of 1930, Unit 8, section NWFP, consulted 22 November 2026.]
